items.text: Personal vengeance is a worthy final purpose for someone who has been gravely wronged.
items.evidence: Her vengeance is abandoned; the redemptive climax is 'a kiss with genuine maternal love', not the destruction of Stefan.

items.text: Someone who has been gravely wronged is morally obliged to answer that wrong with violence.
items.evidence: 'Maleficent refuses to kill Stefan and tries to end the conflict peacefully'; the wrong is answered by love, not violence.

items.text: Vengeance should sometimes be renounced for the sake of peace and the safety of the living.
items.evidence: 'Maleficent refuses to kill Stefan and tries to end the conflict peacefully'; afterwards she 'removes the thorn wall... bringing peace between the two kingdoms.'

items.text: Evil is finally undone not by superior force but by qualities it cannot comprehend, such as love and kindness.
items.evidence: The curse she thought unbreakable ('no power on earth') is undone by love, which 'she and Stefan both believe is nonexistent'; Stefan's iron armies fail.

items.text: Hatred imposed by another's wrong can be laid down rather than carried to the grave.
items.evidence: She lays down her hatred, spares Stefan, removes the thorn wall and restores the Moors.

items.text: Vengeance against those who have wronged you is a legitimate response to injustice.
items.evidence: The revenge curse rebounds on her and must be undone; 'Filled with regret, Maleficent says goodbye to Aurora.'

items.text: Sparing a defeated enemy is a greater victory than killing him.
items.evidence: She spares Stefan at the moment of her advantage; he destroys himself by attacking again and falling from the tower.

items.text: Refusing to kill an enemy who lies at one's mercy is a mark of moral strength rather than of weakness.
items.evidence: Refusing to kill the disarmed Stefan is staged as the culmination of her moral recovery.

items.text: Those who pursue vengeance sacrifice the love that might have saved them.
items.evidence: Stefan's vengeful obsession costs him wife and daughter; Maleficent nearly loses Aurora to her own curse of revenge.

items.text: A ruler gripped by fear of retribution turns that fear into tyranny over his own people.
items.evidence: 'Stefan begins mass-manufacturing iron weapons nonstop and grows obsessed with killing Maleficent to the point of insanity'; he imprisons his own daughter.

items.text: Having suffered an injustice licenses a person to inflict harm on others.
items.evidence: Maleficent's revenge on an innocent child is the film's central wrong, which she must repent and reverse.

items.text: A person who has been gravely violated is entitled to take whatever revenge lies within their power.
items.evidence: Though violated, her taking revenge on Aurora is the act the film treats as a wrong requiring repair.

items.text: Restraint from harm one has both the power and the warrant to inflict is the highest form of power.
items.evidence: With her wings restored and her enemy beneath her, she withholds the killing blow and seeks peace.

items.text: Violence against those who have humiliated you can be a genuine liberation rather than a further degradation.
items.evidence: Her retaliatory curse degrades her into the 'cruel and bitter' ruler of an iron-fisted Moors rather than liberating her.

items.text: Understanding the injury behind a cruel person's cruelty obliges us to spare them.
items.evidence: Aurora, knowing Maleficent cursed her, still frees her wings and stands with her.

items.text: Those who inflict great harm on others have usually suffered great harm themselves.
items.evidence: Maleficent's cruelty follows Stefan's betrayal: 'Infuriated over the betrayal, Maleficent grows cruel and bitter, ruling the Moors with an iron fist'; Jolie: 'at the core it is abuse, and how the abused then have a choice of abusing others or overcoming'.

items.text: Those who do great evil are products of the injury done to them, and their wrongdoing is thereby explicable.
items.evidence: The whole 'feminist revisionist backstory' structure explains the fairy-tale villain's evil by the mutilation/betrayal she suffered — 'What could make a woman become so dark...?'

items.text: A person deeply injured by others can recover the capacity to love rather than being permanently defined by the injury.
items.evidence: Jolie: the abused can 'overcom[e] and remain loving, open people'; Maleficent recovers maternal love after mutilation.

items.text: A person who inflicts harm on others was usually first damaged by forces outside their choosing.
items.evidence: Her turn to cruelty is caused by Stefan drugging her and burning off her wings, an injury inflicted on her, not chosen.

items.text: People are capable of fundamental moral change.
items.evidence: Maleficent moves from cursing an infant to dying-for-her devotion; Phillips notes the film 'is all about second thoughts'.

items.text: Those who harm others are themselves acting out of injury or need, so evil is rarely a pure origin.
items.evidence: Both villains are shown as injured: Maleficent by mutilation, Stefan by ambition and fear; 'evil' is given a prior cause rather than a pure origin.

items.text: Having been wronged and shamed excuses the harm one then does to others.
items.evidence: The curse on an innocent baby is treated as an error Maleficent regrets and tries to undo; Jolie frames the abused as having 'a choice of abusing others or overcoming'.

items.text: Some beings are evil by their very constitution, rather than made so by circumstances that might be reasoned with or reformed.
items.evidence: The premise reworks the fairy tale's constitutional villain into a wronged, recoverable person — 'Long live the feminist revisionist backstory.'

items.text: Those who do evil were first themselves denied love, and this origin is part of the truth about them.
items.evidence: Maleficent's darkness originates in love betrayed — 'Stefan's love overshadowed by his ambition' — and in the loss of her wings.

items.text: A person can genuinely change their fundamental character, and such transformation is the central achievement of a life.
items.evidence: Her transformation from 'Dark Lady' to loving mother is the central action the ending rewards.

items.text: Words spoken in anger bind the speaker as much as the one they are aimed at, and cannot simply be unsaid.
items.evidence: She cannot revoke the curse spoken in fury: 'forgetting she made "no power on earth" able to do so.'

items.text: Those who inflict harm are usually acting out of their own fear and deprivation, and deserve understanding as well as condemnation.
items.evidence: Stefan's obsession is bred of fear of retribution; Maleficent's cruelty of betrayal; the telling asks understanding for the horned 'Dark Lady' while still showing the curse as wrong.

items.text: Having been wronged excuses or lessens the wrong one then commits.
items.evidence: Being violated explains but does not absolve: 'Realizing she does not have the heart to hurt Aurora, Maleficent privately and unsuccessfully attempts undoing Aurora's curse.'

items.text: A person's private failings of anger and pride do not stay private; they extend outward into tyranny over those subject to them.
items.evidence: Both rulers' private wounds become public tyranny: Maleficent 'ruling the Moors with an iron fist', Stefan arming his kingdom nonstop.

items.text: Evil is best understood as an alien force to be eradicated rather than as a distortion of something ordinary and human.
items.evidence: Evil here is a distortion of a loving being: 'Jolie is excellent as the hopeful fairy... also brilliant as the Dark Lady.'

items.text: A person's motives can be transformed over time, so that self-interest gives way to genuine concern for others.
items.evidence: Vengeful self-interest gives way over years of watching Aurora: 'Realizing she does not have the heart to hurt Aurora...'

items.text: Feeling remorse for having wounded those who cared for one is a necessary stage of moral growth.
items.evidence: 'Filled with regret, Maleficent says goodbye to Aurora' — remorse immediately precedes the redemptive kiss.

items.text: Having been made monstrous by injustice excuses a person from responsibility for what they become.
items.evidence: Jolie: the abused 'have a choice of abusing others or overcoming and remaining loving, open people' — responsibility is retained.

items.text: Ambition tempts most sharply those who lack wealth and position, and small corruptions prepare the way for larger ones.
items.evidence: Stefan, a peasant boy, is drawn by 'his ambition to be king'; a first betrayal (the wings) leads to escalating atrocity.

items.text: One and the same person can be genuinely both hero and villain, without either fact cancelling the other.
items.evidence: The same figure is both the curse-laying 'Dark Lady' and the film's rescuing hero, and neither cancels the other.

items.text: Good intentions excuse those who care incompetently for the vulnerable.
items.evidence: The pixies are 'clueless and dangerously careless'; Stefan 'scolds the pixies for failing to protect her.'

items.text: The received account of who was hero and who was villain in the past deserves to be trusted.
items.evidence: The narrator 'reveals herself as the elderly Aurora, the one people called the "Sleeping Beauty"' — the received tale is corrected; critics call it a 'revisionist backstory'.

items.text: The strong owe the weak protection and restraint rather than domination.
items.evidence: She abandons iron-fisted rule for protection: she 'removes the thorn wall, restores the Moors, and crowns Aurora as ruler.'

items.text: Women's proper sphere is domestic, and their presence in labour, arms and rule is a disorder.
items.evidence: Maleficent is 'protector of the Moors' and a combatant; Aurora is crowned ruler — critics call it a feminist revision that 'demolishes stereotypes'.

items.text: The bond between parent and child is the strongest form of love, and it does not depend on blood.
items.evidence: 'Maleficent... kisses her forehead with genuine maternal love, which finally breaks the curse'; the NYT notes 'an astonishing maternal kiss'.

items.text: Romantic love arising suddenly between strangers is a sufficient foundation for the deepest of bonds.
items.evidence: 'Maleficent and Diaval kidnap Prince Philip and sneak into the castle, but Philip's kiss cannot wake her.'

items.text: True love is recognized immediately and requires no knowledge of the other's name or origin.
items.evidence: The near-stranger prince's kiss fails; only the long-nurtured maternal bond breaks the curse.

items.text: Romantic love is the highest good, and a life without the beloved is a life wasted.
items.evidence: Romantic love is displaced as the film's highest good by maternal love, which alone breaks the curse.

items.text: Genuine kindness is owed through ties of blood and flows most reliably through them.
items.evidence: Aurora's blood father imprisons her and rages; her unrelated 'fairy godmother' is the one who cares for and saves her.

items.text: Vows and confidences create real obligations, and betraying them is the paradigmatic wrong.
items.evidence: The originating wrong is the betrayal of intimate trust: the childhood lovers' bond broken by drugging and mutilation.

items.text: Goodness in people is merely a comforting fiction they tell about themselves.
items.evidence: Maleficent and Stefan both 'believe [true love] is nonexistent' — and the film refutes them with the maternal kiss.

items.text: Using other people as instruments for one's own gratification is the root form of wrongdoing.
items.evidence: Stefan exploits Maleficent's love and trust — 'Stefan visits Maleficent and drugs her' — to take her wings as a means to the throne.

items.text: An outsider may rightly intervene in a family's decisions about a child when the family's judgement is failing.
items.evidence: 'Maleficent and Diaval... secretly begin taking over care of her from the incompetent pixies.'

items.text: Cynicism about human motives is a truer view of the world than sentimentality.
items.evidence: The bitter, cynical view of love held by the cursed and the king is overturned by the ending.

items.text: The appetite for power corrupts those who pursue it and destroys the affections that compete with it.
items.evidence: 'Stefan's love overshadowed by his ambition to be king'; later he 'grows obsessed with killing Maleficent to the point of insanity, even refusing to see his wife on her deathbed.'

items.text: The innocent and the uninvolved are shielded from violence directed elsewhere.
items.evidence: The innocent newborn Aurora is the one struck by a curse aimed at her father's betrayal.

items.text: Those who exploit or degrade others eventually come to ruin.
items.evidence: Stefan, who mutilated and betrayed, dies falling from his own tower after attacking again.

items.text: What was taken from a wronged person should be restored to them, not replaced with a substitute.
items.evidence: 'Aurora frees Maleficent's wings' — the stolen wings must be returned; commentary praises the film for letting the woman 'reclaim the story'.

items.text: Protecting the young through deception and confinement, however loving, causes harm and cannot be sustained.
items.evidence: Hiding Aurora with the pixies fails: 'the pixies are eventually forced to tell Aurora the truth... Hurt and betrayed, Aurora confronts Maleficent'; Stefan's imprisonment doesn't stop the curse.

items.text: Deception undertaken to shield a loved one from a painful truth is justified.
items.evidence: The concealment of Aurora's parentage and curse ends in her feeling 'hurt and betrayed' and walking into the spindle.

layers.label: Plot summary
layers.content:
## Plot
Maleficent is a powerful fairy living in the Moors, a magical forest realm. As a child, she meets a human boy named Stefan, and they fall in love with each other. However, as they get older, they grow apart, with Stefan's love overshadowed by his ambition to be king, while Maleficent becomes protector of the Moors.
When King Henry attempts to conquer the Moors, Maleficent mortally wounds him. On his deathbed, he declares whoever kills her will be king. Stefan visits Maleficent and drugs her. Unwilling to kill her, Stefan instead uses a bracelet made of iron, which is lethal to fairies, to burn off her wings and presents them as "proof" of her death. While distraught by her loss, Maleficent saves Diaval, a trapped raven, from a farmer by turning him into a human. Diaval offers his service and tells her of Stefan's coronation. Infuriated over the betrayal, Maleficent grows cruel and bitter, ruling the Moors with an iron fist.
Years later, Diaval informs Maleficent about the christening of Stefan's newborn daughter, Aurora. Maleficent arrives uninvited while three pixies, Knotgrass, Flittle, and Thistlewit, are bestowing magic gifts, and places a curse on Aurora: before the sun sets on Aurora's 16th birthday, Aurora will prick her finger on the spindle of a spinning wheel and fall into a death-like sleep. Maleficent mocks Stefan's plea for mercy, but states Aurora's curse can be broken by true love's kiss, which she and Stefan both believe is nonexistent. Stefan orders the pixies to hide and protect Aurora in a forest cottage until after her 16th birthday. He also destroys every spinning wheel in the kingdom, hiding their remnants in the castle dungeon; he then sends his army after Maleficent, but she surrounds the Moors with a wall of thorns. Over the years, Stefan begins mass-manufacturing iron weapons nonstop and grows obsessed with killing Maleficent to the point of insanity, even refusing to see his wife on her deathbed.
Maleficent and Diaval watch Aurora grow from afar, and secretly begin taking over care of her from the incompetent pixies. After several face-to-face encounters with Maleficent, whom she regards as her "fairy godmother", Aurora bonds with her and regularly visits the Moors. Realizing she does not have the heart to hurt Aurora, Maleficent privately and unsuccessfully attempts undoing Aurora's curse, forgetting she made "no power on earth" able to do so. Meanwhile, Aurora meets Philip, a prince from the neighboring kingdom, and both take a liking to each other.
Before Aurora’s 16th birthday, Maleficent allows her to live in the Moors. However, the pixies are eventually forced to tell Aurora the truth about her family and the curse. Hurt and betrayed, Aurora confronts Maleficent and returns to her father’s castle, where King Stefan imprisons her and scolds the pixies for failing to protect her. As night falls, the curse takes control of Aurora, leading her to a spinning wheel where she pricks her finger and falls into a deep, death-like sleep.
Wanting to save Aurora, Maleficent and Diaval kidnap Prince Philip and sneak into the castle, but Philip’s kiss cannot wake her. Filled with regret, Maleficent says goodbye to Aurora and kisses her forehead with genuine maternal love, which finally breaks the curse and awakens her.
As they try to escape, Stefan and his guards attack them. Maleficent turns Diaval into a dragon, but they are eventually overpowered. Aurora frees Maleficent’s wings, allowing her to fight back. Although Maleficent refuses to kill Stefan and tries to end the conflict peacefully, he attacks her again and falls to his death from the tower.
After Stefan’s death, Maleficent removes the thorn wall, restores the Moors, and crowns Aurora as ruler, bringing peace between the two kingdoms. Aurora also begins a romance with Philip. The narrator reveals herself as the elderly Aurora, the one people called, the "Sleeping Beauty".

layers.label: Critical reception
layers.content:
## Reception > Critical Response
Maleficent received mixed reviews from critics, who praised the performances (especially Jolie's), visual effects and costumes, but criticized the script and Stromberg's direction. The review aggregator website Rotten Tomatoes reported that the film had a 54% approval rating based on 277 reviews, with an average rating of 5.7/10. According to its consensus, "Angelina Jolie's magnetic performance outshines Maleficent's dazzling special effects; unfortunately, the movie around them fails to justify all that impressive effort." On Metacritic, the film has a weighted average score of 56 out of 100 based on 44 critics, indicating "mixed or average reviews". Audiences polled by CinemaScore gave the film an "A" grade on a scale of A+ to F.
The New York Times stated, "with two shorn wings and an astonishing maternal kiss, Maleficent demolishes stereotypes that were only tweaked in Frozen." Kate Taylor of the Globe and Mail was very positive about the film, writing that "[it] surprises not for its baroque visions of a colourful woodland enlivened by joyous fairies and a forbidding castle peopled by unhappy humans, but rather for the thematic richness of its story gloriously personified by Angelina Jolie in the title role." While criticizing the overuse of CGI and 3D effects, she particularly praised the positive message of the film and Jolie's performance. She concluded her review with, "Long live the feminist revisionist backstory." On the contrary, Keith Staskiewicz, writing for the Entertainment Weekly, awarded the film a "B−" and wrote that "there's a lot of levitating cliffs and odd flora. But despite their bleeding-edge digital design, the backgrounds have all the depth of the old matte-painted backgrounds of the analog days," which made the film "[feel] classical in nature." He further commented that "The characters are boiled down to their essentials, the humor is timelessly broad." Michael Philips of the Chicago Tribune gave the film two and a half stars, commenting that the recent "formula" that "a new angle on a well-known fairy tale appears in the light" "works" with Maleficent. He also said that the film "is all about second thoughts" since Maleficent "spends much of the film as Aurora's conflicted fairy godmother." Phillips particularly praised Jolie and Elle Fanning's acting, Rick Baker's makeup (for Jolie's "angular, serrated look"), but criticized James Newton Howard's "sloshy, pushy" musical score. Robbie Collin of The Daily Telegraph wrote, "This Disney reimagining of Sleeping Beauty lacks true enchantment, but Angelina Jolie saves the day." Betsy Sharkey of the Los Angeles Times wrote, "This is Jolie's film because of the Maleficent she makes. Everyone else, even Aurora, fades in her presence." J.C. Maçek III of PopMatters wrote, "Even at its silliest, Maleficent is a well-acted film, with Sharlto Copley turning in a memorable performance and Elle Fanning proving to be an inspired choice for Aurora/Sleeping Beauty. Jolie manages to steal her own show in most every scene. Jolie is excellent as the hopeful fairy, enjoying the world she flies through. She is also brilliant as the Dark Lady, who could be a perfect counterpart to any Darth Vader, as she malevolently takes her revenge on those who have wronged her."
Ann Hornaday of The Washington Post awarded the film three-and-a-half out of four stars, commenting, "Still, for all its limitations, Maleficent manages to be improbably entertaining to watch, due solely to its title character." Writing for Roger Ebert's website, Matt Zoller Seitz awarded Maleficent three out of four stars, praising the themes of the film and the acting of Jolie. Seitz also called the scene in which Maleficent discovers the loss of her wings "the most traumatizing image I've seen in a Hollywood fairy tale since the Christ-like sacrifice of Aslan in 2005's The Chronicles of Narnia: The Lion, the Witch and the Wardrobe." The review in The Globe and Mail further explained that "in the simple context of a fairy tale, Jolie does make both the terrifying horned creature and her gradual awakening heartfelt," extolling the "emotional richness" behind her physical acts. Richard Roeper of the Chicago Sun-Times felt more negatively, assigning it a D. Although Roeper praised the visuals, he criticized the acting and writing, stating that "the story itself might well put you into the same type of coma that befalls the heroine."
Mary Costa, who voiced Aurora in the 1959 animated motion picture, called the film, "a very good movie". She added that "the concept and perspective are totally different than the original film's, which makes it new and interesting." As for Jolie's performance, she said, "No one could have played the part of Maleficent better," concluding that "she was absolutely magnificent!"

## Reception > Rape Allegory
Multiple reviewers and commentators have opined that an early scene in the movie, in which Stefan drugs Maleficent and removes her wings from her unconscious body, is a metaphor for rape. Hayley Krischer of The Huffington Post interpreted the scene as an important reference to rape culture: "This is the horrific side of rape culture. We're so enmeshed in it that it's impossible to ignore a metaphoric rape that occurs in a Disney movie". She went on to praise the film for giving a positive and hopeful message to rape victims, ultimately allowing "the woman to recover. It gives her agency. It gives her power. It allows her to reclaim the story".
Monika Bartyzel of The Week noted the scene's implications in her review: "In its first act, Maleficent offers a dark, surprisingly adult exploration of rape and female mutilation". However, Bartyzel went on to opine that the film portrayed Maleficent's actions as "a rape revenge fantasy" and criticized the film for not following through on its early subtext, ultimately calling it less feminist and reductive compared to its 1959 counterpart: "In Maleficent, Aurora is the product of a cold and loveless marriage and a vengeful, unhinged rapist. Her safety relies on a trio of clueless and dangerously careless fairies, and her Godmother is the woman who cursed her – and who had, in turn, been violated by her own father".
Angelina Jolie addressed the issue during an interview with BBC Radio 4 on the Woman's Hour programme, claiming that the subtext was intentional: "The question was asked: 'What could make a woman become so dark and lose all sense of her maternity, her womanhood, and her softness?' … We were very conscious, the writer and I, that [the scene] was a metaphor for rape". She further explained that the answer to the question "What could bring her back?" was still "an extreme Disney, fun version [of the story]", but "at the core it is abuse, and how the abused then have a choice of abusing others or overcoming and remaining loving, open people".
